title: Data Science Sampler: Beyond Static Plots
text:
Leaflet Interactive Maps
Let’s start with a basic map of earthquakes near New Zealand. We can set the earthquakes to size by magnitude. I messed around with the math a little to get a size ratio that I liked.


Code
data(quakes)

quakes |>
  slice_sample(n = 300) |>
  leaflet() |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.OceanBasemap") |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = ~long,
    lat = ~lat,
    # set circle marker to size by magnitude
    radius = ~mag^2/3,
    # make popup labels
    popup = ~paste0(
      "<strong>Magnitude:</strong> ", mag,
      "<br><strong>Depth:</strong> ", depth, " km"
    ),
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 0.6
  )






Color the points by magnitude and add a legend:


Code
pal <- colorNumeric(
  palette = "viridis",
  domain = quakes$mag
)

leaflet(quakes) |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.OceanBasemap") |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = ~long,
    lat = ~lat,
    radius = ~mag^2/3,
    color = ~pal(mag),
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 0.7
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    "bottomright",
    pal = pal,
    values = ~mag,
    title = "Magnitude"
  )






Now let’s start playing around with the basemaps. You can find all of the possibilities on this website:
https://leaflet-extras.github.io/leaflet-providers/preview/


Code
library(leaflet)
library(dplyr)

data(quakes)

small <- quakes |> filter(mag < 5)
large <- quakes |> filter(mag >= 5)

leaflet() |>
  # Basemaps
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery", group = "Satellite") |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.OceanBasemap", group = "Ocean") |>
  addProviderTiles("Stadia.StamenWatercolor", group = "Artsy") |>

  # Small earthquakes
  addCircleMarkers(
    data = small,
    lng = ~long, lat = ~lat,
    radius = 3,
    color = "blue",
    group = "Smaller quakes",
    stroke = FALSE,
    fillOpacity = 0.5
  ) |>

  # Large earthquakes
  addCircleMarkers(
    data = large,
    lng = ~long, lat = ~lat,
    radius = ~mag * 2,
    color = "red",
    group = "Larger quakes",
    stroke = TRUE,
    weight = 1
  ) |>

  # Layer control
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("Satellite", "Ocean", "Artsy"),
    overlayGroups = c("Smaller quakes", "Larger quakes"),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
  )

title: Data Science Sampler: Beyond Static Plots
text:
Plotly Interactive Plots
Plotly doesn’t change your analysis at all — it just changes how your results exist. It turns a static figure into something you could actually put on a website or share with someone to explore.
Let’s start simple. You make a plot in ggplot and then you feed it into plotly and it’s like magic.


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class,
                     text = paste("Model:", model))) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")






Let’s add more information to the pop-up:


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(text = paste(
      "Model:", model,
      "<br>Class:", class,
      "<br>Displacement:", displ,
      "<br>Highway MPG:", hwy
    )),
    size = 2,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")






Let’s try it with the gapminder data.


Code
p <-  gapminder |> 
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(color="Continent") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 10)) +
  ggtitle("Year: 2007") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






With facets:


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~drv) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






With a boxplot:


Code
p <- ggplot(mpg, aes(class, hwy, fill = class)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






This is my first time doing this with a boxplot, and now this is the only way I’m making a boxplot ever again!
Let’s do it with a line!


Code
economics <- ggplot2::economics

p <- ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






WITH A DENSITY PLOT!


Code
p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, fill = cut)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p)






This is AMAZING! Why am I only just learning this????

title: Data Science Sampler: Beyond Static Plots
text:
Animation
This animation shows the gapminder dataset through time, with GDP per capita on the x-axis and Life expectancy on the y-axis. The points are colored by continent and sized by population (on a log scale).


Code
p <- ggplot(
  gapminder,
  aes(
    x = gdpPercap,
    y = lifeExp,
    group = country,
    color = continent,
    size = pop
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 10)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Year: {frame_time}",
    x = "GDP per capita",
    y = "Life expectancy",
    color = "Continent",
    size = "Population"
  ) +
  transition_time(year)

animate(
  p,
  nframes = 60,
  fps = 4,
  width = 600,
  height = 400,
  renderer = gifski_renderer(),
  device = "ragg_png"
)


You may be able to tell by how many plots I made with the others and how few animations I have given you, that my heart isn’t really in animations. This single animation took about 50% of the time I spent making this. They can be a real pain. A good animation is absolute gold, but it is very hard to make a good animation.

section: Spatial Data - but not people data
text:
Spatial Data - but not people data


Code
library(terra)
library(tidyterra)
library(cmocean)
library(ggthemes)
library(wesanderson)

volcano_df <- as.data.frame(volcano) |>
  mutate(y = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(-y, names_to = "x", values_to = "elevation") |>
  mutate(x = as.numeric(gsub("V", "", x)))

ggplot(volcano_df, aes(x, y, fill = elevation)) +
  geom_raster() + #not the way I choose to do this anymore, but workable for smaller data
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="thermal") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Topographic-style raster map")









Here is some code from my Data Science Across Disciplines class this last January looking at instrumented seal data from the Southern Ocean.
First, some data prep. You are not expected to understand this part.


Code
seal_data <- read_csv("~/Dropbox/!middlebury/Teaching/DSAD 1230/DSAD_2026/R_code/MEOP_data_analysis/data/regional_data/par_seal_data.csv")
seal_data_surface <- seal_data |>
  filter(level==1)

raster_dir <- "/Users/caseysmith/Dropbox/!Middlebury/Teaching/DSAD 1230/DSAD_2025/R_code/Argo_vis_shiny_app"

PacSec_bathy <- rast(paste0(raster_dir, "/data/raster/PacSec_bathy.tif"))


#adjust seal data
seal_data_surface <- seal_data_surface |>
  mutate(lon_anti=case_when(lon<0 ~ lon+360,
                            lon>=0 ~lon))

seal_data_mod <- seal_data |>
  mutate(lon_anti=case_when(lon<0 ~ lon+360,
                            lon>=0 ~lon))

world <- map_data("world")


First a map with “raster” data.


Code
raster_dir <- "/Users/caseysmith/Dropbox/!Middlebury/Teaching/DSAD 1230/DSAD_2025/R_code/Argo_vis_shiny_app"

PacSec_bathy <- rast(paste0(raster_dir, "/data/raster/PacSec_bathy.tif")) 

ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=PacSec_bathy) +
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="gray",
                     limits=c(-6000,0),
                     breaks=c(-6000,-5000,-4000,-3000,-2000,-1000,0),
                     labels=c("-6","-5","-4", "-3","-2","-1", "0")) +
  geom_polygon(data = world, 
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill="white", color="white") +
   labs(fill="Depth (km)",
       x="Longitude", y="Latitude") +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE, xlim = c(140,220), ylim=c(-70,-55) ) +
  ggtitle("Zoomed in on AAR/PAR, Bathymetry") +
  theme_tufte()









Code
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=PacSec_bathy) +
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="gray",
                     limits=c(-6000,0),
                     breaks=c(-6000,-5000,-4000,-3000,-2000,-1000,0),
                     labels=c("-6","-5","-4", "-3","-2","-1", "0")) +
  geom_polygon(data = world, 
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill="white", color="white") +
  geom_point(data=seal_data_surface, 
             aes(x=lon_anti, y=lat, color=TEMP_ADJUSTED), 
             alpha=0.3, size=2) +
  scale_color_cmocean(name="thermal") +
  labs(fill="Depth (km)", color="Temp",
       x="Longitude", y="Latitude") +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE, xlim = c(140,220), ylim=c(-70,-55) ) +

Code
NPP_stack <- rast("~/Dropbox/!Research/Projects/PacAntRidge/data/NPP_raster_stack.nc")

invisible(capture.output({ #to suppress the #$^*@$ progress bar
NPP_stack[NPP_stack >100] = 100 #set max value
NPP_stack[NPP_stack <0] = NA #transform placeholder NA value (-99) to actual NA
}))

#my favorite palette from the wesanderson package
pal <- wes_palette("Zissou1", 100, type = "continuous")
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=NPP_stack[[15]]) + #index to show layer 15 only
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors=pal, limits=c(0,100)) +
  geom_spatraster_contour(data=PacSec_bathy, breaks=c(0,-3000)) + #contour to show margins of mid ocean ridge
  labs(fill="NPP",
       x = "Longitude",
       y = "Latitude") +
  xlim(130, 230) +
  ylim(-70, -55) +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE) +
  theme_tufte() +

Code
#calculate the difference between the two years, by subtracting one from the other
diff_layer <- NPP_stack[[14]]-NPP_stack[[15]]

diff_layer[diff_layer > 75] = 75 #set max value
diff_layer[diff_layer < (-75)] = -75 #set min value


ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data=diff_layer) + 
  scale_fill_cmocean(name="balance", limits=c(-75,75)) + #change to diverging palette
  geom_spatraster_contour(data=PacSec_bathy, breaks=c(0,-3000)) +
  labs(fill="NPP",
       x = "Longitude",
       y = "Latitude") +
  xlim(130, 230) +
  ylim(-70, -55) +
  coord_sf(expand=FALSE) + #set this argument so that it doesn't add a border between the map and the axes
  theme_tufte() +
  ggtitle("NPP difference 2010-2011 minus 2011-2012")

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
For this course, you will need to install both R and RStudio on your computer.

R is the programming language that runs your code.
RStudio is the program we will use to write and run R code.

Install R first, then install RStudio.

1. Install R
Go to the R Project download page.

Mac

Click Download R for macOS.
Download the appropriate installer for your Mac.
Open the downloaded .pkg file and follow the installation instructions.







Tip



If you are unsure which R version you need, click on the Apple in the upper lefthand corner of your desktop and select “About This Mac”, this will contain information both about the chip in your Mac (Intel or M) and the OS that you are running which will allow you to select the correct version of R.




Windows

Click Download R for Windows.
Click install R for the first time.
Click Download R-4.6.1 for Windows (the exact R version number may have changed).
Open the downloaded installer and accept the default installation options.




2. Install RStudio Desktop
Go to the RStudio Desktop download page.

Download the free version of RStudio Desktop for your operating system.
Open the installer.
Follow the installation instructions.



3. Make sure everything works
Open RStudio.



Credit: moderndive


If the installation was successful, you should see the RStudio interface with a Console pane containing some text about your version of R and a > prompt.
At the > prompt, type:

2 + 2

If R responds with:
[1] 4
you’re ready for class!
If you are stumped by 3. Don’t worry about it. If you didn’t get any errors during installation and can open the program ok, then you should be good to go.

title: Intro to R and RStudio
text:
If you have not already, please refer to the Installation Guide to install R and RStudio on your computer.
R (The brain behind it all)
RStudio (The interface you work with)
RStudio is an IDE (Integrated Development Environment) that gives you a user-friendly interface to write and run your R code.
When you open RStudio, you should see something similar to this:

title: Intro to R and RStudio
text:
1️⃣ Open Your .qmd File in RStudio
Navigate to the file on your local computer and click to open it!

Some folks prefer to use the “Files” tab within RStudio to navigate to the file
Other folks prefer to interact with their files in their typical way (Using Finder on Mac or File Explorer on PC)

Either way works just fine!

title: Intro to R and RStudio
text:
2️⃣ Install Quarto in RStudio
Option 1: Using the RStudio Interface

Go to the Packages pane in RStudio (bottom-right by default),
Click Install,
In the box that appears:

Enter the package name (quarto),

Make sure Install dependencies is checked,
Click Install.



Option 2: Using R Code in the Console

install.packages("quarto")

title: Intro to R and RStudio
text:
3️⃣ Render and Preview
Click the Render button () at the top-right of your RStudio editor window.
Tada! You now have created a .html file!
The file has been created in the same folder as your .qmd file: 
When you render, a preview of the document will show up!






Tip



By default, the preview of .html will pop up in your web browser. This is totally okay. In fact, I tend to prefer this approach when I’m working at a computer station with multiple monitors.
However, you may prefer to have the .html preview in your viewer pane right within RStudio. This is what I prefer when I’m just working on just my laptop.
Click on the “gear button”  and select “Preview in Viewer Pane”


The preview will update whenever you re-render the document.
